newsitem.title: TURKEY: Kurd jail riot as Turkey offensive continues.
newsitem.headline: Kurd jail riot as Turkey offensive continues.

text.p: A hospital official said on Wednesday 11 people died in a prison riot by rebel Kurds that erupted as Turkish forces pressed an offensive against Kurdish guerrillas in the mountainous east of the country.

"We know the identity of eight of the dead, and we are trying to identify the other three," a Diyarbakir hospital official told reporters. The eight identified were members of the Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK), he said.
However, Justice minister Sevket Kazan said a total of nine prisoners had died in the riot, the state-run Anatolian news agency reported.
The prison riot came as troops attacked PKK rebels in the mountains of eastern Tunceli province. Security officials in Tunceli said troops had killed at least 27 rebels in the past three days.

"We actually think the death toll for the PKK is more than 27 as we have heard that the PKK have been throwing their dead into a stream," an army official told Reuters. "From listening to wireless conversations we believe around 20 PKK dead are lying in the stream."
He said one soldier had died and an officer was injured.

Following the prison riot, witnesses in Diyarbakir said security forces barred movement in or out of the hospitals and prison. Prisoners' relatives crowded outside the hospital, chanting and making victory signs. Skirmishes broke out between families and the police.

The hospital official said around 10 people also were injured in the riot, sparked by a prisoner protest against the government's failure to improve prison conditions after a nationwide hunger strike in July.
The pro-PKK DEM news agency said 20 people were hurt and called it a premeditated attack: "Soldiers and police mounted an attack against the PKK prisoners of war."
DEM quoted hospital sources as saying many of the wounds were from bullets, makeshift skewers and wooden beams.
The state-run Anatolian said the inmates died of blows but no bullets were fired. It blamed the Kurdish inmates.

"These inmates suddenly began to attack and beat up (security staff) when they were taken out for exercise," Anatolian quoted a Diyarbakir official as saying. "And some of them broke down the doors of other wards and tried to increase participation in a kind of rebellion."
The official said the riot escalated when staff intervened to prevent prisoners opening other wards. He said some prisoners had been protesting against transfers to another prison.
Turkish prison officials complain that sprawling wards allow inmates to form groups and take control, rioting at changes of regulations or attempts to move gang members to other prisons.

More than 20,000 people have died since 1984 in clashes between government forces and rebels in a war that costs Turkey an estimated $8 billion annually. Successive governments have refused to discuss demands for Kurdish self rule.
The European Parliament last week threatened to block millions of dollars of aid to Turkey because of its human rights record.

Amnesty International will test Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's promises to improve rights and solve the Kurdish issue through "Moslem brotherhood". The head of the London-based rights group is due in Turkey on Thursday hoping to see Erbakan although the government has not yet agreed to a meeting.
